title: Words You Know by Sight
bigQuestion: How do readers get so fast that they never have to stop?

story.title: Marcus Reads the Whole Page
story.kicker: One boy, one book, one page. He reads it all the way through. Then somebody claps.
paragraphs: Marcus is in first grade. He has a book about a dog. Last week he got stuck on every line. He had to sound out the word 'the' again and again. It was slow. His little sister Nia got bored and walked away.

Tonight Marcus tries the same book. He sits on the couch. Nia sits next to him. He reads the first line. He does not stop. He reads the next line. The word 'said' is there. He knows it. He keeps going.
Marcus reads the whole page without stopping. He even makes the dog sound happy. He looks up. Nia is clapping. 'Read it again!' she says. So he does. This time it is even faster.
What changed? Marcus did not get a new brain. He learned some words by heart. He read the same book a few times. Now the words are his. This chapter shows you how to make words yours too.
story.think: Is there a book you know so well that you can read it fast? What makes it easy?

lessons.title: Words That Come Up Everywhere
lessons.mainIdea: Some words come up so often that you should know them the second you see them.
reading: Look at this line. 'The cat sat on the mat and you sat too.' Count the word 'the.' It is there two times. Count 'and.' Count 'you.' These words show up on almost every page.
A word you know the second you see it is a *sight word*. You do not sound it out. You just know it. The, and, you, is, to, a. Readers see these words so much that they learn them by heart.
Knowing sight words makes you fast. If you stop at 'the' every time, reading is slow. If you know 'the' on sight, you zoom right past it. Then you can save your energy for the hard words.

words.d: a word you know right away without sounding it out

look.title: Counting Words on One Page
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a page written for this lesson
look.prompt: Which word came up the most? Why would it help to know that word on sight?

check.q: What is a sight word?
choices: A word you sound out slowly
A word you know right away
check.why: A sight word is one you know the second you see it. You do not need to sound it out.

check.q: Why does knowing 'the' on sight help you?
check.why: If you know 'the' right away, you zoom past it. That makes reading faster.

check.q: Which word shows up on almost every page?
check.why: Words like 'and,' 'the' and 'you' come up all the time. 'Zebra' and 'rocket' do not.

lessons.title: Tricky Words
lessons.mainIdea: Some words do not follow the sound rules, so you learn them by heart.
reading: Try to sound out the word 'said.' S-a-i-d. It should sound like 'sayd.' But it does not. We say 'sed.' The word 'said' breaks the rules. So does 'was.' So does 'of.'
A word that does not follow the sound rules is a *tricky word*. You cannot sound it out. You have to learn it by heart. Look at it. Say it. Write it. Then you own it.
Here is a trick. Find the part that plays fair. In 'said,' the s and the d play fair. Only the middle is odd. Remember the odd part. Then the word is easy.

words.d: a word that does not follow the sound rules

look.title: Three Words That Cheat
look.text: Look at these three words: said, was, of. Try to sound each one out. 'Was' should sound like 'wass.' But we say 'wuz.' 'Of' should sound like 'off.' But we say 'uv.' They do not play fair.
look.prompt: Pick one tricky word. Which part of it plays fair? Which part is odd?

check.q: Why is 'said' a tricky word?
choices: It does not sound the way it looks
check.why: 'Said' looks like 'sayd' but we say 'sed.' It does not follow the sound rules.

check.q: How do you learn a tricky word?
choices: Sound it out one letter at a time
Look at it, say it and write it
check.why: Tricky words cannot be sounded out. You learn them by heart by looking, saying and writing.

check.q: Which word is a tricky word?
check.why: 'Of' does not follow the rules. We say 'uv.' 'Cat' and 'sun' sound just the way they look.

lessons.title: The -at Family
lessons.mainIdea: Words that end the same way are a family, and one family helps you read many words.
reading: Read these words: cat, hat, bat, mat, sat. Look at the end of each one. It is 'at' every time. Only the first letter changes. If you can read 'cat,' you can read all of them.
Words that share an ending are a *word family*. The -at family has cat and hat. The -ing family has ring, sing and king. The -ake family has cake, lake and bake.
A word family is a shortcut. Learn one ending. Then swap the first letter. C-at. H-at. B-at. That is three words for the price of one. Families make reading fast.

words.d: a group of words that share the same ending, like cat, hat and bat

look.title: Building the -ake Family
look.text: Start with 'cake.' Cover the c. What is left? 'ake.' Now put an l in front. Lake. Put a b in front. Bake. Put an r in front. Rake. Same ending, four words.
look.prompt: What other letter could you put in front of 'ake' to make a real word?

check.q: Which word is in the -at family?
check.why: 'Mat' ends in 'at,' so it belongs to the -at family. 'Map' and 'mud' do not.

check.q: What stays the same in a word family?
check.why: In a word family, the ending stays the same. Only the first part changes.

check.q: You can read 'sing.' Which new word can you read now?
check.why: 'King' is in the -ing family with 'sing.' Just swap the first letter.

lessons.title: Adding -s, -ed and -ing
lessons.mainIdea: A small ending on a word changes when it happened or how many there are.
reading: One dog. Two dogs. Add an s and you get more than one. One cat, two cats. One hat, two hats. The little s at the end means 'more than one.'
Now look at 'jump.' I jump today. I jumped yesterday. I am jumping right now. The word is the same. Only the *ending* changes. The ending tells you when it happened.
When you see a long word, look for an ending. Take it off. 'Jumping' is jump plus ing. 'Wanted' is want plus ed. Read the small word first. Then add the ending back.

words.d: letters added to the end of a word, like -s, -ed or -ing

look.title: One Word, Three Days
look.text: Look at Ana with a ball. Yesterday she kicked the ball. Today she kicks the ball. Right now she is kicking the ball. Same girl, same ball, same word. The ending changed each time.
look.prompt: Which ending tells you it already happened? Which one tells you it is happening now?

check.q: What does adding -s to 'dog' tell you?
choices: There is more than one dog
check.why: Adding -s means more than one. 'Dogs' means two or more dogs.

check.q: Which word tells you something already happened?
check.why: The -ed ending means it happened before. 'I jumped yesterday.'

check.q: What small word is inside 'wanted'?
check.why: Take off the -ed ending and you find 'want.' Read the small word first.

lessons.title: Two Words Make One
lessons.mainIdea: Some long words are really two small words stuck together.
reading: Look at the word 'sunset.' It looks long. But cover the end. You see 'sun.' Cover the start. You see 'set.' Sunset is just sun plus set. Two words, stuck together.
A word made from two smaller words is a *compound word*. Bedroom is bed plus room. Cupcake is cup plus cake. Rainbow is rain plus bow. You already know both parts.
When you see a long word, look for two words inside. Read the first one. Read the second one. Put them together. Snow plus man. Snowman. Now the long word is easy.

words.d: a word made of two smaller words, like sunset or bedroom

look.title: Words in the Kitchen
look.text: Look around a kitchen. There is a cupcake on the table. There is a teapot on the stove. There is a doorbell by the door. Each thing has a long name. Each name is really two small words.
look.prompt: Pick one kitchen word. What are the two small words inside it?

check.q: Which word is a compound word?
check.why: 'Rainbow' is rain plus bow. Two small words make one long word.

check.q: What two words are inside 'bedroom'?
check.why: 'Bedroom' is bed plus room. Both are real words you already know.

check.q: How do you read a compound word?
choices: Read each small word, then join them
check.why: Find the two small words inside. Read each one. Then put them together.

lessons.title: Read Like You Talk
lessons.mainIdea: Good reading sounds like talking, not like a robot.
reading: Listen to a robot read. 'The. Dog. Ran. To. The. Park.' Every word stops. Now listen to a friend read it. 'The dog ran to the park!' The words flow. That is *smooth* reading.
Reading with feeling is called *expression*. If the story says 'Help!' you say it loud. If a boy is sad, your voice sounds sad. A question goes up at the end. Do you hear it?
Look at the marks. A period means stop for a tiny breath. A question mark means make your voice go up. An exclamation point means say it with big feeling. The marks tell you how to read.

words.d: flowing along with no bumps or stops
reading with feeling in your voice

look.title: Two Ways to Read One Line
look.text: Here is a line: 'Look out! The ball is coming!' Read it one way. Say every word flat and slow. Now read it again. Say it loud and fast, like you mean it. Which one sounds like a real person?
look.prompt: What does the exclamation point tell you to do with your voice?

check.q: What does smooth reading sound like?
check.why: Smooth reading flows like talking. The words do not stop and start.

check.q: What should your voice do at a question mark?
check.why: A question mark tells you to make your voice go up at the end.

check.q: The story says 'Help!' How should you read it?
check.why: An exclamation point means say it with big feeling. 'Help!' should sound loud and urgent.

lessons.title: Read It Again
lessons.mainIdea: Reading the same book again makes you faster each time.
reading: Marcus read his dog book once. It was slow. He read it again. It was better. He read it a third time. Now he did not stop at all. The same book got easier every time.
This is called *rereading*. Reading a book again is not cheating. It is practice. The first time, you work hard on the words. The next time, the words are already in your head.
Pick a book you like. Read it today. Read it tomorrow. Read it to a pet or a little sister. Each time, you get faster. Each time, you sound better. That is how readers grow.

words.d: reading the same book or page again

look.title: How Long Marcus Took
look.cite: counted for this lesson from a made-up page
look.prompt: What happened to the time each time Marcus read the page? Why?

check.q: What happens when you reread a book?
check.why: Each time you read the same book, the words are more familiar. You get faster.

check.q: Is reading a book again cheating?
check.why: Rereading is practice, not cheating. It is how readers get strong.

check.q: Why was Marcus's third read so fast?
choices: The words were already in his head
check.why: After two reads, Marcus knew the words. They were already in his head.

review.q: Which word should you know on sight?
review.why: 'The' comes up on almost every page. Readers learn it by heart.

review.q: Which word does not follow the sound rules?
review.why: 'Was' looks like 'wass' but we say 'wuz.' It is a tricky word.

review.q: Cat, hat and bat are in the same what?
review.why: They all end in 'at.' Words with the same ending are a word family.
The -ed ending means before. 'Jumped' means it happened already.
'Snowman' is snow plus man. Both are words you know.

review.q: What is the best way to get faster at a book?
review.why: Rereading puts the words in your head. Each read is faster.
